nameStory: The Christmas anemone gets its festive name from its beautiful red and green coloration that resembles traditional holiday colors. When fully expanded with its tentacles spread wide, it looks like a colorful underwater Christmas ornament decorating the rocky seafloor. It's also called the painted anemone for its striking mottled patterns that look like they were hand-painted by an artist.
description: The Christmas anemone is a large, solitary sea anemone that looks like a colorful underwater flower attached to rocks. These remarkable creatures can live up to 80 years, making them some of the longest-lived animals in New England's coastal waters. They're typically reddish with green mottling and have dozens of thick tentacles surrounding a central mouth. Christmas anemones are surprisingly large for intertidal creatures, often growing several inches across when fully expanded.

idTips.label: Colorful mottled pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive red, green, and sometimes orange coloration in irregular patches across the body, like a hand-painted design that gives it the 'painted anemone' nickname

idTips.label: Thick, sturdy tentacles
idTips.description: Tentacles feel substantial and meaty to the touch (if gently touched), not thin or delicate like some other anemones - they're arranged in rings around the central mouth

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Much bigger than most tide pool anemones you'll encounter - often several inches across when fully opened, making it hard to miss

idTips.label: Solitary lifestyle
idTips.description: Always found alone, never in clusters or groups like some other anemone species - each one claims its own rocky territory

idTips.label: Firm attachment
idTips.description: Base feels very securely attached to rock surfaces - won't budge easily when gently prodded, unlike some anemones that can move around

idTips.label: Retracts when disturbed
idTips.description: Quickly pulls in tentacles and becomes a bumpy, closed blob when touched or when waves crash over it, then slowly reopens when calm returns

habitat: Christmas anemones live in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal waters along New England's coast, especially in tide pools and on wave-exposed rocky shores. They prefer areas with good water circulation and attach themselves firmly to hard surfaces like granite ledges, boulders, and rocky crevices. You'll most often spot them in the lower intertidal zone where they're covered by water most of the time but exposed during very low tides.

seasonality.spring: Most active and fully expanded as water temperatures begin to warm, making this an excellent time for observation during low tides when they're exposed and feeding.
seasonality.summer: Fully active and easiest to observe, with bright colors most vivid. Low tide exploration during summer offers the best viewing opportunities in tide pools and on rocky shores.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may be less expanded during the cooler months. Colors remain vibrant and they continue feeding actively before winter.
seasonality.winter: Less active in the coldest months but still present and observable during winter low tides, though they may remain more contracted than in warmer seasons.

funFact: Christmas anemones can live for up to 80 years, meaning some of the individuals you see today in New England tide pools were already adults when your grandparents were children - they're like underwater time capsules that have witnessed decades of coastal changes!
confusionNotes: Christmas anemones are most easily confused with Dahlia anemones, and both are sometimes called 'northern red anemones.' The key difference is that Christmas anemones have more distinct mottled coloration with greens mixed in, while Dahlia anemones tend to be more uniformly reddish. Remember: Christmas = colorful like holiday decorations, Dahlia = more uniform like a single flower color.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Christmas' anemone, this species is found year-round and the name refers only to its colors, not its seasonal appearance. The scientific name 'Urticina' comes from the Latin word for nettle, referring to the stinging cells in their tentacles, though their sting is generally too mild to be felt by humans.
compareHints: Since Christmas anemone is the only Urticina species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other large anemones in the region. It's much more colorful than the common green anemone and significantly larger than most frilled anemones. Its mottled red and green pattern is unique among New England's sea anemones, making it one of the easiest to identify once you know what to look for.
